summary: Defines a way to carry one IP datagram as the payload inside another IP datagram. This is useful for tunneling, such as delivering traffic to a mobile device that is away from home.

eli5.summary: It is like putting a letter in a bigger envelope with a new address on the outside. The post office reads only the outer address.

questions: what is ip in ip encapsulation
how to tunnel ip packets inside ip
why use encapsulation instead of ip source routing
subtitle: How to wrap one IP datagram inside another so it can be steered to a tunnel exit point.

tldr.problem: Sometimes a datagram must be delivered to an intermediate node that the original destination address would never select, for example to reach a mobile node away from home.
tldr.mechanism: The encapsulator inserts an outer IP header (protocol 4) before the original datagram. The decapsulator at the tunnel exit strips it off and delivers the original datagram.
tldr.outcome: IP in IP is a simpler and better-behaved alternative to the loose source route option, at the cost of larger datagrams. The text was later updated by RFC 3168 and RFC 6864.

today: RFC 2003 is a Proposed Standard, and it has been updated by RFC 3168 and RFC 6864. It was written with Mobile IP (RFC 2002) in mind as one use.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 2003 specifies how an IP datagram can be carried as the payload of another IP datagram. The goal is to alter normal routing: the datagram is delivered to an intermediate destination that would not be chosen from the network part of the original Destination Address.

Once the encapsulated datagram reaches that intermediate node, it is decapsulated, giving back the original datagram, which is then delivered to the address in its original header. This is often called tunneling. The encapsulator is the entry point of the tunnel and the decapsulator is the exit point. In the general case the source, encapsulator, decapsulator and destination are four separate nodes.
sections.eli5: Imagine a letter that has to take a detour through a friend's house first. You put it in a bigger envelope addressed to the friend. The friend opens it and mails the inner letter on.

sections.title: Why Encapsulate Instead of Source Route
sections.content:
The Mobile IP working group uses encapsulation to carry datagrams from a mobile node's home network to an agent that can deliver them locally to the node at its current location. The RFC also lists multicasting, preferential billing, choice of routes with selected security attributes and general policy routing as possible uses.

The IP loose source routing option can often achieve a similar effect, but the RFC gives reasons to prefer encapsulation: unsolved security problems with source routing, performance problems when routers forward datagrams with IP options, nodes that process source routes incorrectly, firewalls that may exclude source-routed datagrams, complications for authentication, and the impoliteness of routers modifying datagrams they did not originate.

There are two drawbacks. Encapsulated datagrams are typically larger than source-routed ones, and encapsulation only works if the tunnel exit is known in advance to be able to decapsulate.
sections.eli5: The old trick of scribbling extra directions on the letter itself confuses many post offices and gets letters stopped. A new outer envelope is cleaner, but it makes the parcel bigger.

sections.title: The Outer IP Header
sections.content:
To encapsulate, the encapsulator inserts an outer IP header before the datagram's existing IP header. The outer Source and Destination Addresses are the tunnel endpoints (the encapsulator and the decapsulator). The inner header keeps the original sender and recipient. The inner header is not changed except that its TTL is decremented as described below, and its options are not changed in transit.

Key outer fields: Version is 4, Protocol is 4, and TOS is copied from the inner header. Total Length covers the outer header, the inner header and its payload. If the Don't Fragment bit is set in the inner header, it MUST be set in the outer header. Options in the inner header are in general not copied to the outer header.

On TTL: when encapsulation is part of forwarding, the inner TTL is decremented by one. An encapsulator MUST NOT encapsulate a datagram with TTL = 0, and a decapsulator MUST discard a datagram whose inner TTL is 0 after decapsulation. The inner TTL is not changed when decapsulating.

To prevent loops, a router MUST NOT tunnel a datagram whose source address matches one of its own interface addresses, or matches the tunnel destination. Such datagrams SHOULD be discarded.
sections.eli5: The big envelope has its own stamp and address. The inner letter stays exactly as it was, except that a countdown counter on it is lowered by one when it is forwarded, so letters that wander in circles eventually get thrown away.

sections.title: ICMP Messages from Within the Tunnel
sections.content:
Routers inside the tunnel report problems to the encapsulator, because the outer header names it as the sender. The encapsulator may relay a similar ICMP message to the original sender, after stripping the outer header from the returned copy of the datagram.

What to do depends on the message. Datagram Too Big MUST be relayed. Host Unreachable SHOULD be relayed. Protocol Unreachable is turned into a Destination Unreachable with Code 0 or 1, since the original sender never used protocol 4. Port Unreachable should never arrive and MUST NOT be relayed. Source Route Failed and Redirect MUST NOT be relayed. Source Quench SHOULD NOT be relayed; instead the encapsulator should use its own congestion control. Time Exceeded, which signals a presumed loop inside the tunnel, MUST be reported to the sender as Host Unreachable (Type 3, Code 1).
sections.eli5: If the big envelope gets stuck, the problem report goes back to the person who sealed it, not to the letter writer. That person decides which news to pass on and rewrites it so it makes sense to the writer.

sections.title: Tunnel Management and Soft State
sections.content:
ICMP only requires routers to return 8 octets of the datagram beyond the IP header, which is not enough to include the inner IP header. So the encapsulator cannot always relay an error. To cope, it SHOULD keep soft state per tunnel: the MTU of the tunnel, the TTL (path length) of the tunnel, and the reachability of the tunnel end. Later datagrams are checked against that state, and if one would violate it the encapsulator sends an ICMP error to the original sender and still forwards the datagram into the tunnel.

For MTU, all encapsulators MUST support Path MTU Discovery soft state within their tunnels. The MTU reported to the original sender SHOULD be the tunnel MTU minus the size of the encapsulating IP header. The RFC prefers fragmenting the original datagram at the encapsulator over letting the encapsulated datagram be fragmented, because then the decapsulator would have to reassemble before decapsulating.

On congestion, the encapsulator SHOULD reflect it in its soft state and use appropriate congestion control, and SHOULD NOT send Source Quench to the original sender.
sections.eli5: The person sealing envelopes keeps a notebook about each route: how big a parcel fits, how many stops it has, and whether the far end answers. The notebook lets them answer questions without waiting for fresh news.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC warns that IP encapsulation potentially reduces Internet security. Border routers cannot filter on the usual header fields because the original addresses, protocol and transport port numbers are no longer in their normal positions, and any datagram can be tunneled.

Routers need to understand encapsulation and ideally integrate filtering with IP authentication. Encapsulated packets without authentication are a potentially large risk. Encapsulated and encrypted datagrams can be filtered only by a router that shares the security association.

Hosts able to receive encapsulated datagrams SHOULD admit only those that are harmless, come from an authentically identified trusted source, include an IP Authentication header inside, or are addressed to an interface of the decapsulator or a node with which it has a special relationship. Router checks should be a backup, not the only check.
sections.eli5: A guard who checks the address on each envelope is fooled when the real address is hidden inside a bigger envelope. So the guard must open or verify the big envelopes, and the receiver should accept them only from people it trusts.

viz.caption: HOW THE ENCAPSULATOR TREATS ICMP FROM THE TUNNEL

items.label: Datagram Too Big
items.desc: MUST be relayed to the original sender.

items.label: Protocol Unreachable
items.desc: Sent on as Destination Unreachable with Code 0 or 1.

items.label: Port Unreachable
items.desc: Should never arrive; MUST NOT be relayed.

items.label: Source Route Failed
items.desc: Handled by the encapsulator; MUST NOT be relayed.

items.label: Source Quench
items.desc: SHOULD NOT be relayed; use congestion control.

items.label: Redirect
items.desc: MAY be handled by the encapsulator; MUST NOT be relayed.

items.label: Time Exceeded
items.desc: MUST be reported as Host Unreachable (Type 3, Code 1).
